15. ANALYSING THE FLOW

In section 13, we constructed a continuous vector field X on the closed surface S. Since in this setting S is in ideal position, its vertical sublamination A°s projects via a : M — S to a geodesic lamination A c S.

Together, X and A have the following properties:

- the vector field X is tangent to the geodesic lamination A;
- the vector field is zero at a point p if and only if 7-' (p) is a center circle and we refer to these as the critical points;
- each critical point lies on an isolated geodesic in A and we call these geodesics the critical geodesics;
- each critical geodesic contains exactly one critical point;
- at each critical point, the index of X at p is in (-1,0, +1); moreover, if we consider a small disk D centered at p and split D along the critical geodesic to produce two half-disks, then the index of X at p is in 1],0, 7} on each of the half-disks.

Item (3) is given by lemma 9.1 and item (5) by lemma 13.1.

The plan now is to first excise the non-isolated leaves of A from S, producing a surface with boundary So c S where An So consists only of isolated geodesic arcs, each of which is compact. We then split So into a number of "regions" R; by cutting along the "critical arcs." By applying the Poincaré-Hopf theorem to the vector field X restricted to a region Ri, we show that at least one of these regions has positive Euler characteristic and therefore must be a topological disk. Its pre-image (R) must contain half of a vertical leaf of 9", and this causes a contradiction, completing the overall proof.

For simplicity, we assume that the continuous vector field X integrates to a flow on S and we explain in the following remark how to adapt the proof when this is not the case.

Remark. The definition of a dumbbell and the proof of proposition 14.1 do not actually rely on X integrating to a flow o on all of S. We can instead define an outflow edge d as having a small neighborhood U such that any integral curve starting at a point x € U and tangent to X must remain in U until it hits o. The proof of proposition 14.1 only considers the flow o on the lamination I. In our setting. I will be a geodesic lamination and so the flow is well defined. After applying the proposition and restricting to a subset So eS, we may replace X by a smooth approximation such that X is unchanged on the finitely many arcs of An So which contain critical points. Thus, we may freely assume that X integrates to a flow d.

Let I be the sublamination of A consisting of all of the non-isolated leaves in

A. Apply proposition 14.1 to I and let So denote the subset S\int(K) given by the proposition. Each boundary component of So is therefore a dumbbell.
